claim: Many marine animals, ranging from corals to fishes, synchronise reproduction to lunar cycles.
source: Many marine animals, ranging from corals to fishes, synchronise reproduction to lunar cycles.
evidence: This is a general statement about marine animal behavior presented in the introduction without specific data from this study, but supported by the broader literature context.

claim: In the annelid Platynereis dumerilii, reproductive timing is orchestrated by an endogenous monthly (circalunar) clock entrained by moonlight.
source: In the annelid Platynereis dumerilii, this timing is orchestrated by an endogenous monthly (circalunar) clock entrained by moonlight.
evidence: This statement is supported by prior research cited in the manuscript and forms the basis for the current study.

claim: Maturation elicits large transcriptomic and proteomic changes in Platynereis heads.
source: Whereas maturation elicits large transcriptomic and proteomic changes, the circalunar clock exhibits only minor transcriptomic, but strong proteomic regulation.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript showing differential expression analysis results.

claim: The circalunar clock exhibits only minor transcriptomic regulation in Platynereis heads.
source: Whereas maturation elicits large transcriptomic and proteomic changes, the circalunar clock exhibits only minor transcriptomic, but strong proteomic regulation.
evidence: This is supported by the RNA-Seq differential expression data showing only 0.12% of transcripts regulated by circalunar phase.

claim: The circalunar clock exhibits strong proteomic regulation in Platynereis heads.
source: Whereas maturation elicits large transcriptomic and proteomic changes, the circalunar clock exhibits only minor transcriptomic, but strong proteomic regulation.
evidence: This is supported by proteomic data showing 24.53% of quantifiable proteins regulated by circalunar phase.

claim: Prepro-whitnin/proctolin is a circalunar clock target in Platynereis.
source: Examples include prepro-whitnin/proctolin and ependymin-related proteins as circalunar clock targets.
evidence: This is supported by differential expression data and in situ hybridization showing circalunar regulation of this neuropeptide.

claim: Ependymin-related proteins are circalunar clock targets in Platynereis.
source: Examples include prepro-whitnin/proctolin and ependymin-related proteins as circalunar clock targets.
evidence: This is supported by differential expression data showing multiple ependymin-related proteins regulated by circalunar phase.

claim: Circadian and circalunar clock effects are likely distinct.
source: It corroborates that circadian and circalunar clock effects are likely distinct and identifies key molecular brain signatures for reproduction, sex and circalunar clock phase.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of circalunar effects with known circadian clock effects from the literature and the distinct patterns observed.

claim: Laboratory research on Platynereis dumerilii has revealed evidence for internal monthly timers.
source: Laboratory research on animals such as the marine annelid Platynereis dumerilii or the marine midge Clunio marinus has indeed revealed evidence for such internal timers, showing that nocturnal light (in nature provided by the moon) does not only impact directly on transcription (Zantke et al., 2015), but is both necessary and sufficient to entrain endogenous monthly (circalunar) oscillators (Kaiser et al., 2016; Zantke et al., 2013), which in turn orchestrate reproduction at distinct times of the lunar month (Figure 1a).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Nocturnal light is both necessary and sufficient to entrain endogenous monthly (circalunar) oscillators in Platynereis.
source: Laboratory research on animals such as the marine annelid Platynereis dumerilii or the marine midge Clunio marinus has indeed revealed evidence for such internal timers, showing that nocturnal light (in nature provided by the moon) does not only impact directly on transcription (Zantke et al., 2015), but is both necessary and sufficient to entrain endogenous monthly (circalunar) oscillators (Kaiser et al., 2016; Zantke et al., 2013), which in turn orchestrate reproduction at distinct times of the lunar month (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is supported by cited previous research on circalunar clock entrainment.

claim: The Platynereis brain plays a crucial role in circadian and circalunar timing.
source: Importantly, the bristleworm brain also plays a crucial role in circadian and circalunar timing (Hauenschild, 1956a; Hauenschild, 1956b; Hauenschild, 1959; Hauenschild, 1960; Hauenschild, 1966; Hofmann, 1976; Hofmann and Schiedges, 1984; Schenk et al., 2016; Zantke et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Tails of decapitated Platynereis animals undergo sexual maturation within two weeks but are no longer synchronised to the lunar phase.
source: Its importance in reproductive timing is highlighted by the fact that tails of decapitated animals undergo sexual maturation within two weeks, but are no longer synchronised to the lunar phase (Hauenschild, 1966; Hauenschild, 1974; Schenk et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous experimental work.

claim: The Platynereis brain possesses non-visual photoreceptors that likely receive light inputs for circalunar (and circadian) clock entrainment.
source: The brain also possesses non-visual photoreceptors that likely receive light inputs for circalunar (and circadian) clock entrainment (Arendt et al., 2004; Tessmar-Raible et al., 2007; Zantke et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on photoreceptors.

claim: The Platynereis brain integrates information on maturation, sexual differentiation, and circalunar phase to bring about lunar-synchronised reproduction.
source: Taken together, these findings argue that the Platynereis brain integrates information on maturation, sexual differentiation, and circalunar phase in order to bring about lunar-synchronised reproduction.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited literature and the rationale for the current study.

claim: The transcript levels of a subset of core circadian clock genes are influenced by the phase of the circalunar oscillator in Platynereis.
source: First, we systematically assessed transcriptome signatures, building on our previous observation that the transcript levels of a subset of core circadian clock genes are influenced by the phase of the circalunar oscillator in Platynereis, a finding that has also been observed in corals and the reef fish Siganus guttatus (Raible et al., 2017; Altincicek and Vilcinskas, 2007 references cited therein).
evidence: This is supported by previous observations cited in the manuscript.

claim: Maturation induces the largest amount of changes on both transcriptome and proteome levels in Platynereis heads.
source: This systematic approach revealed that maturation induces the largest amount of changes on both transcriptome and proteome levels, whereas the circalunar clock has a much stronger impact on the proteome than the transcriptome.
evidence: This is directly supported by the differential expression analysis data presented in the results.

claim: The circalunar clock has a much stronger impact on the proteome than the transcriptome in Platynereis heads.
source: This systematic approach revealed that maturation induces the largest amount of changes on both transcriptome and proteome levels, whereas the circalunar clock has a much stronger impact on the proteome than the transcriptome.
evidence: This is supported by comparing the percentages of differentially expressed transcripts (0.12%) versus proteins (24.53%) for circalunar phase.

claim: Ependymin-related proteins are strongly affected on both transcript and protein levels by maturation and circalunar clock phases.
source: Specifically, we demonstrate that Ependymin-related proteins (ERPs) are strongly affected on both transcript and protein levels by maturation and circalunar clock phases.
evidence: This is supported by differential expression data for ERPs shown in the results section.

claim: Whitnin/Proctolin is regulated by the circalunar clock in Platynereis.
source: We further show that the neuropeptide Whitnin/Proctolin, which recently has been correlated with the spawning event in the semilunar spawner abalone Haliotis asinina (York et al., 2012), is also regulated by the circalunar clock in Platynereis.
evidence: This is supported by differential expression data and in situ hybridization results.

claim: The primary assembly (Pdu_HeadRef_TS_v1) consisted of 407,172 transcripts with >200 bp.
source: Our primary assembly (Pdu_HeadRef_TS_v1) was systematically curated to (i) remove redundancies, (ii) merge scaffold information provided by published Platynereis sequences, (iii) remove sequence contaminations (e.g. prokaryotic), and (iv) flag additional sequences with high similarity to other species (see Materials and methods section), resulting in our final reference sets (Pdu_HeadRef_TS_v4 and v5, see Figure 2, Figure 2—source data 1–3 and Materials and methods section).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2.

claim: The final reference set Pdu_HeadRef_TS_v5 contains 52,059 transcripts.
source: These, together with 83 transcripts spiking in one sample (IM_NM) discovered during data processing for differential expression analysis (see below) were then removed to generate the final Pdu_HeadRef_TS_v5 assembly containing 52,059 transcripts.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing transcriptome assembly.

claim: Maturation exhibits 8,598 differentially expressed transcripts (16.52% of all transcripts).
source: Of the three major comparison groups, that is maturation, sex biased and circalunar, maturation exhibits the largest number of DETs (Altincicek and Vilcinskas, 2007); 16.52% of all transcripts, Figure 3a).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Sexual differentiation was characterised by 640 differentially expressed transcripts (1.23%).
source: Sexual differentiation was characterised by 640 DETs (1.23%), whereas 63 DETs (0.12%) appear to distinguish the two sampled phases of the circalunar clock.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing differential expression analysis.

claim: 63 differentially expressed transcripts (0.12%) distinguish the two sampled phases of the circalunar clock.
source: Sexual differentiation was characterised by 640 DETs (1.23%), whereas 63 DETs (0.12%) appear to distinguish the two sampled phases of the circalunar clock.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing differential expression analysis.

claim: Of the 640 sex-biased differentially expressed transcripts, 149 (23.28%) were also regulated by maturation.
source: Of the 640 sex-biased DETs, 149 (23.28%) were also regulated by maturation and six (0.94%) by the circalunar phase (Figure 3—source data 3–5); of the 63 circalunar DETs 34 (53.97%) were also regulated by maturation.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing overlap between different comparison groups.

claim: Of the 640 sex-biased differentially expressed transcripts, six (0.94%) were regulated by the circalunar phase.
source: Of the 640 sex-biased DETs, 149 (23.28%) were also regulated by maturation and six (0.94%) by the circalunar phase (Figure 3—source data 3–5); of the 63 circalunar DETs 34 (53.97%) were also regulated by maturation.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing overlap between different comparison groups.

claim: Of the 63 circalunar differentially expressed transcripts, 34 (53.97%) were also regulated by maturation.
source: Of the 640 sex-biased DETs, 149 (23.28%) were also regulated by maturation and six (0.94%) by the circalunar phase (Figure 3—source data 3–5); of the 63 circalunar DETs 34 (53.97%) were also regulated by maturation.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing overlap between different comparison groups.

claim: Four transcripts were regulated in all three parameters (maturation, sex, and circalunar phase).
source: Four transcripts were regulated in all three parameters (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3a Venn diagram.

claim: The quantitative sequencing results generally validated well when assessed by qRT-PCR on independent samples.
source: These experiments showed that the differences observed in our sequencing approach generally validated well when assessed by qRT-PCR on independent samples (Figure 4a–d, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR validation data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The circalunar candidate differentially expressed transcripts appeared more variable in qRT-PCR validation.
source: Within these experiments, the tested circalunar candidates appeared more variable (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This observation is based on qRT-PCR validation data.

claim: The majority of circalunar candidate differentially expressed transcripts exhibited generally lower overall expression levels.
source: We noted that the majority of circalunar candidate DETs exhibited generally lower overall expression levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and showed additional susceptibility to strain specific polymorphisms or phase differences in their circalunar rhythm profiles, similar to previous findings (Zantke et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on observation of expression data and comparison to previous findings.

claim: Maturation, sexual differentiation and circalunar timing can be clearly distinguished on a molecular level.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that maturation, sexual differentiation and circalunar timing – while being tightly coordinated processes - can be clearly distinguished on a molecular level and are likely driven by different biological mechanisms.
evidence: This is inferred from the distinct GO-term enrichments and differential expression patterns observed for each process.

claim: Maturation, sexual differentiation and circalunar timing are likely driven by different biological mechanisms.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that maturation, sexual differentiation and circalunar timing – while being tightly coordinated processes - can be clearly distinguished on a molecular level and are likely driven by different biological mechanisms.
evidence: This is inferred from the distinct molecular signatures observed for each process.

claim: A total of 2,290 proteins with at least two unique peptides identified per protein were identified from experimental samples.
source: In total we identified 2,290 proteins with at least two unique peptides identified per protein from our experimental samples.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing proteomic analysis.

claim: The correlation between normalised log10-transformed transcriptome and proteome expression values showed a Pearson-correlation coefficient of 0.482.
source: This showed a significant, but relatively low correlation (cor.test()) Pearson-correlation coefficient of 0.482 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The relatively low correlation between transcript and protein levels is highly consistent with previous transcriptome-proteome comparisons studies.
source: This relatively low correlation between transcript and protein levels is highly consistent with previous transcriptome-proteome comparisons studies.
evidence: This is supported by comparison to literature values from other organisms.

claim: A total of 1,064 quantifiable proteins were defined for robust comparison between all conditions.
source: To enable robust comparison between all conditions, we defined a subset of 'quantifiable protein' comprising only those detected uniquely in at least 2 BR and in 3 out of the 5 TR per BR for all samples, yielding a total of 1,064 proteins; a number comparable to studies of the mosquito Aedes aegypti head proteome, applying similar stringency filters (1,139 proteins, Nunes et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing proteomic analysis.

claim: 693 proteins (65.13% of quantifiable proteins) were differentially expressed over the process of maturation.
source: As for the transcriptome data, the largest proportion of proteins, that is 693 proteins were differentially expressed over the process of maturation, corresponding to 65.13% of quantifiable proteins (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5a.

claim: Sexual differentiation accounted for only 17 differentially expressed proteins (1.60%).
source: Contrary to the transcriptome profiling results, however, sexual differentiation accounted for only 17 differentially expressed proteins (DEP, 1.60%).
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing proteomic differential expression.

claim: Circalunar phase affected 261 differentially expressed proteins (24.53%).
source: Conversely, circalunar phase affected 261 DEP (24.53%), significantly exceeding the amount observed in the transcriptomic analysis.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing proteomic differential expression.

claim: Of the 17 sex biased proteins, 12 were regulated during maturation.
source: Of the 17 sex biased proteins, 12 were regulated during maturation, as were 177 of the 261 (67.82%) circalunar proteins.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing overlap between proteomic comparison groups.

claim: Of the 261 circalunar proteins, 177 (67.82%) were regulated during maturation.
source: Of the 17 sex biased proteins, 12 were regulated during maturation, as were 177 of the 261 (67.82%) circalunar proteins.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing overlap between proteomic comparison groups.

claim: Six proteins were affected by all three processes (maturation, sex, and circalunar phase).
source: Six proteins were affected by all three processes (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5a Venn diagram.

claim: Only 40.12% (278 out of 693) of maturation differentially expressed transcripts showed a similar profile of regulation on the protein level.
source: A comparison between protein and RNA expression clusters for the maturation process revealed similar dynamic groups (Figure 3b vs. 5b), however, these were not necessarily populated by corresponding transcripts and proteins, as only 40.12% (278 out of 693) of DETs showed a similar profile of regulation on the protein level.
evidence: This is stated in the results section comparing transcriptome and proteome clustering.

claim: Transcript to protein changes are 'offset' in time for the majority of the transcripts during maturation.
source: This finding suggests that transcript to protein changes are 'offset' in time for the majority of the transcripts.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that only 40.12% of maturation DETs showed similar regulation at protein level.

claim: Out of a total of 2,448 GO terms present in all 2,290 detectable proteins, 121 GO terms were enriched.
source: GO enrichment analysis of the DEPs showed that out of a total of 2,448 GO terms present in all 2,290 detectable proteins, 121 GO terms were enriched.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing GO-term analysis of proteins.

claim: Of the 121 enriched GO terms in proteins, 75 (62.5%) were found in maturation differentially expressed proteins.
source: Of these, 75 (62.5%) GO terms were found to be enriched in maturation DEPs, 17 in sex biased DEPs, and 46 in circalunar DEPs.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing GO-term enrichment in proteins.

claim: Of the 121 enriched GO terms in proteins, 17 were found in sex biased differentially expressed proteins.
source: Of these, 75 (62.5%) GO terms were found to be enriched in maturation DEPs, 17 in sex biased DEPs, and 46 in circalunar DEPs.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing GO-term enrichment in proteins.

claim: Of the 121 enriched GO terms in proteins, 46 were found in circalunar differentially expressed proteins.
source: Of these, 75 (62.5%) GO terms were found to be enriched in maturation DEPs, 17 in sex biased DEPs, and 46 in circalunar DEPs.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing GO-term enrichment in proteins.

claim: There was little overlap between the GO term enrichments across the three different analysed biological processes in the proteome.
source: Like for the transcriptome, there was little overlap between the GO term enrichments across the three different analysed biological processes (Figure 5c, Figure 5—figure supplements 2–6, Figure 5—source data 10–13).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by figures showing GO-term enrichment.

claim: A second round of proteomic analysis on independent immature samples led to a set of 1,671 quantifiable proteins.
source: This second round (filtered as above) led to a set of 1,671 quantifiable proteins (Figure 5—source data 14), out of which 1,017 were also present in the initial (1,064 quantifiable proteins) dataset, thus 95.58% of the proteins initially passing our stringent quality filter criteria again passed these criteria, indicating a high reliability and reproducibility of protein detection for this sample type.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the second proteomic analysis.

claim: 95.58% of the proteins initially passing stringent quality filter criteria again passed these criteria in the second proteomic analysis.
source: This second round (filtered as above) led to a set of 1,671 quantifiable proteins (Figure 5—source data 14), out of which 1,017 were also present in the initial (1,064 quantifiable proteins) dataset, thus 95.58% of the proteins initially passing our stringent quality filter criteria again passed these criteria, indicating a high reliability and reproducibility of protein detection for this sample type.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the second proteomic analysis.

claim: Of the 1,671 proteins in the second dataset, 173 (10.35%) were significantly differentially expressed between circalunar phases.
source: Of the 1,671 proteins of the new dataset, 173 (10.35 %, Figure 5—source data 15) were significantly differentially expressed.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the second proteomic analysis.

claim: Whitnin is the mollusc orthologue of the insect neuropeptide Proctolin.
source: Whitnin is the mollusc orthologue of the insect neuropeptide Proctolin (Veenstra, 2010, Figure 7—figure supplement 1, Figure 7—source datas 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by citation and phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Prepro-whitnin was shown to be differentially regulated on transcript level in the nervous system of abalone Haliotis asinina over the course of two weeks, with maximal expression just prior to semi-circalunar spawning events.
source: Of note, prepro-whitnin was shown to be differentially regulated on transcript level in the nervous system of abalone Haliotis asinina over the course of two weeks. Maximal expression occurred just prior to the semi-circalunar spawning events of this organism (York et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research on abalone.

claim: Ependymin-related proteins are a group of small extracellular glycoproteins originally identified as one of the most abundant proteins in teleost-fish cerebrospinal fluid.
source: Ependymin-related proteins (ERPs) are a group of small extracellular glycoproteins originally identified as one of the most abundant proteins in teleost-fish cerebrospinal fluid (Shashoua, 1991; Suárez-Castillo and García-Arrarás, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on ependymins.

claim: Ependymin-related proteins were considered to be vertebrate specific until recently.
source: Later, ERPs were discovered in other vertebrates and due to their complete absence from all ecdysozoan genomes and transcriptomes analysed so far, were considered to be vertebrate specific (Suárez-Castillo and García-Arrarás, 2007; Andrews et al., 1992) references cited therein).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous reviews.

claim: Ependymin-related proteins have been identified in an increasing number of non-ecdysozoan invertebrates, including echinoderms, hemichordates, molluscs, annelids and even cnidarians.
source: However, recently ERPs have been identified in an increasing number of non-ecdysozoan invertebrates, including echinoderms, hemichordates, molluscs, annelids and even cnidarians (Hall et al., 2017; Suárez-Castillo and García-Arrarás, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent research.

claim: A recurring feature of ependymin-related proteins is their multiple group-specific gene duplications.
source: A re-occurring feature of ERPs are their multiple group-specific gene duplications (Hall et al., 2017; Suárez-Castillo and García-Arrarás, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: 15 ependymin-like sequences were identified in the Platynereis transcriptome.
source: We identified 15 ependymin-like sequences in the transcriptome, most of which cluster together in one specific subgroup (Figure 6a, Figure 6—figure supplement 1, Figure 6—source datas 1 and 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Seven Platynereis ependymin-related proteins were detected in the proteome, all of which were significantly differentially abundant between the two circalunar phases.
source: Seven Pdu-ERPs were detected in the proteome, all of which were significantly differentially abundant between the two circalunar phases (Figure 5—source data 18).
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing ependymin-related proteins.

claim: Two Platynereis ependymin-related proteins showed correlated changes between transcript and proteome level.
source: Of those, two showed correlated changes between transcript and proteome level (Figure 6b,b' and Figure 6—figure supplement 2) and were subsequently investigated for their expression patterns.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6.

claim: Both investigated Platynereis ependymin-related proteins exhibited identical expression patterns, covering sensory appendages of the head.
source: Both Pdu-erps exhibited identical patterns, covering sensory appendages of the head; palpae and peristomial cirri, a large expression domain on the ventral side of the head, as well as an anterior and posterior domain in the dorsal brain (Figure 6c–e, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown by in situ hybridization images.

claim: Pre-pro-whitnin is expressed in four main regions in Platynereis heads.
source: Pre-pro-whitnin is expressed in four main regions. Besides expression in single cells of the peristomial cirri, it is expressed in two areas located in the medial forebrain (Figure 7a',a''), and one small paired cluster slightly anterior to and below the anterior pair of adult eyes (Figure 7a''').
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown by in situ hybridization images in Figure 7.

claim: Myohaemerythrin was present in the medial brain and to a lesser part around the posterior eyes.
source: Similarly, myohr was present in the medial brain and to a lesser part around the posterior eyes (Figure 7b'b'').
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown by in situ hybridization images in Figure 7.

claim: Ferritin showed a broad expression in the Platynereis head.
source: Different to whitnin and myohr, ferritin showed a broad expression in the head (Figure 7c',c'').
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown by in situ hybridization images in Figure 7.

claim: The effect of the circalunar clock is not confined to specific regions of the head or brain.
source: The fact that the expression domains are already largely divergent among these few investigated circalunar candidates, suggests that the effect of the circalunar clock is not confined to specific regions of the head or brain.
evidence: This is inferred from the diverse expression patterns of circalunar-regulated genes.

claim: About 17 percent of all analysed transcripts undergo regulation during maturation in Platynereis heads.
source: Using this protocol for Platynereis dumerilii, we find that ~ 17 percent of all analysed transcripts and ~66% of the analysed proteins undergo regulation during maturation.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion summarizing the main findings.

claim: About 66% of the analysed proteins undergo regulation during maturation in Platynereis heads.
source: Using this protocol for Platynereis dumerilii, we find that ~ 17 percent of all analysed transcripts and ~66% of the analysed proteins undergo regulation during maturation.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion summarizing the main findings.

claim: The maturation process is the biggest driving force for changes on both transcriptome and proteome levels as Platynereis worms approach spawning.
source: This indicates that the maturation process is the biggest driving force for changes on both transcriptome and proteome levels as worms approach the single circalunar-synchronised spawning event of their lifecycle.
evidence: This is inferred from the large proportion of transcripts and proteins regulated during maturation.

claim: The head is a major source of factors that orchestrate the maturation transition in Platynereis.
source: While this process is accompanied by major morphological changes in the trunk (in particular, the generation of germ cells that amass to up to 40% of the body mass, accompanied by a deprivation of up to 60% of longitudinal muscle fibres), the head is known to be a major source of factors that orchestrate this transition (Hauenschild, 1956a; Hauenschild, 1956b; Hauenschild, 1966; Hofmann, 1976; Schenk et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The observed changes in the Platynereis head transcriptome and proteome strongly support the notion that the head orchestrates maturation.
source: The observed changes in the head transcriptome and proteome strongly support this notion, and the recent identification of a major brain hormone component that regulates maturation onset and progression (Schenk et al., 2016) provides an interesting entry point to understand how these significant changes are hormonally regulated and conveyed to the entire body.
evidence: This is inferred from the large-scale molecular changes observed in the head during maturation.

claim: Maturation of Platynereis is accompanied by a significant increase of overall eye volume.
source: Maturation of Platynereis is also accompanied by a significant increase of overall eye volume (Fischer and Brökelmann, 1966).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: A significant increase in transcript abundance of the Platynereis r-opsin1 gene was observed during maturation.
source: In line with the described expansion of the outer segments of the eye photoreceptors – that typically harbour the photopigments – we observed a significant increase in transcript abundance of the Platynereis r-opsin1 gene, a major opsin gene expressed in the adult eye photoreceptors (Arendt et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by data and citation.

claim: The circalunar phase has little impact on transcript expression changes in Platynereis heads (only 0.12% of transcripts regulated).
source: Specifically, we find that only 0.12% of the transcripts we analysed are regulated.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion summarizing the circalunar transcriptome findings.

claim: The circalunar transcriptome regulation (0.12%) is more than 20-fold less than the impact of the circadian clock on brain/head transcriptome regulation in several animals.
source: This is more than 20-fold less than what has been shown as an impact of the circadian clock on the regulation for brain/head transcriptome in several animals, for example Aedes aegypti (6.7%, Leming et al., 2014), Drosophila melanogaster (2.8%, Hughes et al., 2012) and Mus musculus (3–4%, Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion comparing circalunar effects to circadian effects from the literature.

claim: The proteomic changes observed between two different circalunar time points in Platynereis are comparable to the circadian changes observed in the nervous system of other animals.
source: Thus, the proteomic changes we observe between two different circalunar time points (with a similar number of quantifiable proteins) are comparable to the circadian changes observed in the nervous system of other animals.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion comparing circalunar proteomic effects to circadian proteomic effects from the literature.

claim: The mechanisms responsible for circalunar reproductive timing possibly operate and might be coordinated more strongly at post transcriptional, translational/post-translational level(s), than on transcript level(s).
source: This implies that, differing from the known circadian clock studies, the circalunar oscillator has a significantly stronger impact on the proteome than on the transcriptome. Thus, the mechanisms responsible for circalunar reproductive timing possibly operate and might be coordinated more strongly at post transcriptional, translational/post-translational level(s), than on transcript level(s).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that circalunar phase has much stronger impact on proteome than transcriptome.

claim: Animals were housed in a 1:1 mixture of Natural Sea water (NSW) and Artificial Sea water (ASW, 30 ‰ Tropic Marine).
source: Platynereis dumerilii were housed in plastic boxes and kept in a 1:1 mixture of Natural Sea water (NSW) and Artificial Sea water (ASW, 30 ‰ Tropic Marine).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing animal husbandry.

claim: Worms were exposed to a circadian light regime of 16 hr:8 hr light:dark regime.
source: Worms were either grown in open culture rooms, or in isolated shelf systems and exposed to a circadian light regime of 16 hr:8 hr light:dark regime (Figure 1a), following classical culture conditions (Hauenschild and Fischer, 1969), with a circalunar light regime consisting of nocturnal illumination constituting full moon (FM) provided for eight nights, every 21 days (see below for detailed light conditions).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section and shown in Figure 1a.

claim: The circalunar light regime consisted of nocturnal illumination constituting full moon provided for eight nights, every 21 days.
source: Worms were either grown in open culture rooms, or in isolated shelf systems and exposed to a circadian light regime of 16 hr:8 hr light:dark regime (Figure 1a), following classical culture conditions (Hauenschild and Fischer, 1969), with a circalunar light regime consisting of nocturnal illumination constituting full moon (FM) provided for eight nights, every 21 days (see below for detailed light conditions).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section and shown in Figure 1a.

claim: Pools of 6 heads per biological replicate were sampled at Zeitgeber time 4 for all analyses.
source: For all analyses, pools of 6 heads per biological replicate were sampled at Zeitgeber time 4.

claim: 85.1% of the genes predicted to be present by Cegma were present full length in the transcriptome assembly.
source: Finally, the completeness of our RNA-Seq assembly was tested using Cegma (v2.5, Parra et al., 2007), revealing that 85.1% of the genes predicted to be present were present full length, and 93.6% were present either full length or partially.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing transcriptome assembly quality.

claim: Transcripts passing a Benjamin-Hochberg false discovery rate of 10% were considered as significant in differential expression analysis.
source: Transcripts passing a Benjamin-Hochberg (BH) false discovery rate (FDR) of 10% were considered as significant (FDR, Benjamini and Hochberg, 1995).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing differential expression analysis.
